context: \subsection{Fixed-committee threshold conditions} The relevant quorum principle is standard Byzantine quorum intersection~\cite{byzantinequorums}. For $n$ fixed identities, at most $f$ Byzantine witnesses, and threshold $q$, require \begin{equation} 2q-n>f, \qquad q\le n-f.\label{eq:general-quorum} \end{equation} The first inequality gives an honest identity in every pairwise intersection: $|Q_1\cap Q_2|\ge2q-n>f$. A returned signature at that identity binds a durable branch and slot. If the inequality fails, two quorums can intersect only at faulty identities, so intersection alone cannot prevent conflicting certificates. The second inequality permits a threshold using only honest identities. Both can hold exactly when $n>3f$: necessity follows from $2(n-f)>n+f$, and sufficiency follows by choosing $q=n-f$. This is a threshold feasibility condition, not a liveness theorem. The implementation instantiates $(n,f,q)=(4,1,3)$; the enumerator checks other parameters without claiming their protocol implementation.
